summary.text: The front matter of WHO policy guidance on using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) to diagnose pulmonary tuberculosis. It includes the cover, cataloguing data with ISBN, copyright and disclaimer notices, and a table of contents covering methods, results of the systematic review, cost-effectiveness and recommendations. It also contains acknowledgements and lists of contributors. It ends with the declarations of interest of Guideline Development Group members and the planned review date of 2020.

blocks.title: Executive summary
blocks.content:
Executive summary
Background
World Health Organization’s (WHO’s) End TB Strategy calls for the early diagnosis of tuberculosis 
(TB) and for universal drug-susceptibility testing, highlighting the critical role of laboratories in the 
post-2015 era in rapidly and accurately detecting TB and drug resistance.1 Molecular assays based 
on nucleic acid amplification techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction, have been developed 
for rapid TB diagnosis and are being implemented in developing countries. Loop-mediated 
isothermal amplification (LAMP) is a unique, temperature-independent technique

summary.text: Summarizes the TB-LAMP policy guidance, explaining the End TB Strategy's call for early diagnosis and how the manual LAMP assay works and can be read under ultraviolet light. It recounts the 2012 Guideline Development Group review and the newer evidence assessment. It then states the conditional recommendations for using TB-LAMP instead of, or after, sputum-smear microscopy, together with remarks limiting their scope.

blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a large-scale public health problem. Key global priorities for TB care and 
control include improving case-detection and detecting patients earlier, particularly patients with 
smear-negative TB disease. In 2014, only 63% (6 million) of an estimated 9.6 million people who 
developed TB were reported to WHO, meaning that globally 37% of the estimated cases of TB 
are undetected. WHO has identified the development and evaluation of new diagnostic tools as a 
necessary part of further efforts.3
WHO’s End TB Strategy calls for the early diagnosis of TB and for universal d

summary.text: Sets out the background to TB-LAMP, noting that a large share of TB cases worldwide go undetected and that new diagnostics are a priority. It describes the commercial Eiken assay, its modest infrastructure needs and its history of WHO review. It then walks through the TB-LAMP workflow, from sample preparation and heating to visual reading of fluorescence and waste disposal.

blocks.content: Schematic diagram of the molecular principles of TB-LAMP (Figure 1): coloured DNA strands with primer-binding regions labelled F1, F2, F1c, F2c, B1, B2, B1c and B2c pass through numbered stages (8)–(11) linked by arrows in a cycle. Loop (dumbbell and hairpin) structures form at the strand ends and are elongated into long zigzag products made of alternately inverted repeats of the target sequence.

Photograph of a strip of eight reaction tubes under ultraviolet light (Figure 2): the four tubes on the left are clear, while the four on the right show bright green fluorescence at the bottom, illustrating negative and positive TB-LAMP results.

Workflow diagram of TB-LAMP made of photographs joined by arrows (Figure 3). Steps: collect 60 µl from the sputum cup using an Eiken disposable pipette into a heating tube; heat on a heating block at 90 °C for 5 min; attach and shake the adsorbent tube; fit the injection cap; add 30–35 µl (between lines) to reaction tubes containing dried reagents; close lids and let stand upside down for 2 min; mix; run the LAMP reaction at 67 °C for 40 min; and detect the fluorescent signal.

blocks.title: Evidence synthesis
blocks.content:
In accordance with WHO’s standards for assessing evidence when formulating policy 
recommendations, the GRADE approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development 
and Evaluation, see http://www.gradeworkinggroup.org/) was used. GRADE provides a structured 
framework for evaluating the accuracy of diagnostic tests and their impact on patients and public 
health. 
The evaluation used the GRADE system to determine the quality of the evidence and provide 
information on the strength of the recommendations using PICO questions agreed by the GDG. 
PICO refers to the following four elements

summary.text: Explains that the GRADE approach and PICO-framed questions were used to assess the evidence on TB-LAMP. It lists the four review questions on accuracy versus microscopy, use as an add-on test, comparison with Xpert MTB/RIF, and rates of invalid results.

blocks.title: Criteria for considering studies for this review
blocks.content:
The review included all prospective studies that evaluated the use of TB-LAMP on sputum samples 
from adults with signs and symptoms consistent with pulmonary TB that were conducted in 
settings with an intermediate or high burden of TB. All included studies were conducted after 1 
January 2012, using the final, design-locked TB-LAMP protocol that had been modified by the 
manufacturer. Twenty studies were identified, including all studies that were directly conducted by 
FIND (the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics) or funded through FIND following a request 
for applications (RFAs). T

summary.text: Defines which TB-LAMP studies were eligible for the systematic review, including prospective studies after 2012 in intermediate- and high-burden settings and a supplementary literature search. It lists exclusion criteria for studies and individual participants and describes the culture-based reference standards and smear microscopy definitions used.

blocks.title: Data collection and analysis
blocks.content:
For studies conducted by or funded through FIND, study protocols, inclusion criteria and definitions 
were provided by FIND along with data on individual participants. Further review of the individual-
level data was performed to verify that the study and individual participants met eligibility criteria. 
For studies not affiliated with FIND, individual-level data were requested from the investigators and 
reviewed by at least two authors to determine whether data met the criteria for inclusion in the 
review.
For each study, the minimum data required for each individual enrolled were:

summary.text: Describes how individual-level data were obtained from FIND-affiliated and other TB-LAMP studies, listing the minimum and optional variables collected. It then outlines how accuracy, incremental yield and invalid result rates were calculated and how heterogeneity was assessed.

blocks.title: Guideline Development Group meeting
blocks.content:
Following the initial GDG meeting on TB-LAMP in 2012, a GDG meeting was convened by WHO 
in January 2016 to review the evidence from 20 new studies, of which 13 studies conducted 
in 11 countries met the inclusion criteria. The guideline methodologist participated in the initial 
planning and scoping and in the development of the key questions for the GDG meeting but did 
not participate in the meeting.
The WHO Steering Group was responsible for scoping the guideline, drafting the PICO questions 
and overseeing evidence retrieval and analyses. The Steering Group was also responsible for

summary.text: Notes that a WHO Guideline Development Group met in January 2016 to review 20 new TB-LAMP studies, 13 of which met inclusion criteria, and outlines the roles of the methodologist and Steering Group.

blocks.title: Scope
blocks.content:
3. Scope
This document provides a pragmatic summary of the evidence and recommendations on using 
TB-LAMP to diagnose pulmonary TB in adults with signs and symptoms consistent with TB. It 
should be read in conjunction with the WHO’s 2015 framework for implementing TB diagnostics, 
which provides guidance on implementing the diagnostic tools and methods approved by WHO 
within the context of a country’s infrastructure, resources, epidemiology and in the presence of 
drug-resistant TB and HIV.9 http://www.who.int/tb/publications/implementing_TB_diagnostics/en/

summary.text: States that the guidance summarizes evidence and recommendations on using TB-LAMP for pulmonary TB in symptomatic adults and should be read with WHO's 2015 framework for implementing TB diagnostics.

blocks.title: Target audience
blocks.content:
This guidance is intended to be used by clinicians treating patients with TB, and managers and 
laboratory directors working in TB programmes, in coordination with external laboratory consultants, 
donor agencies, technical advisers, laboratory technicians, procurement officers for laboratory 
equipment, service providers in the private sector, relevant government sectors, and implementation 
partners that are involved in country-level strengthening of TB diagnostic and treatment services. 
Individuals responsible for programme planning, budgeting, mobilizing resources and implementing 
traini

summary.text: Identifies the intended users of the TB-LAMP guidance, from clinicians and laboratory directors to donors, procurement officers and programme planners.

blocks.title: Evidence base for policy formulation
blocks.content:
Of the 20 studies identified that evaluated TB-LAMP, 13 studies conducted in 11 countries met 
the criteria for inclusion in the systematic review (Fig. 4). Six studies were excluded because it was 
unclear whether participants had been receiving TB treatment within 60 days prior to enrolment. 
One study was excluded because rapid speciation testing on positive mycobacterial cultures was 
not performed. (Annex 1 comprises references to the studies identified for the systematic review of 
the diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP.)
Of the 20 studies identified as evaluating TB-LAMP, 10 had not been pu

summary.text: Describes the evidence base for the TB-LAMP recommendations: of 20 studies identified, 13 in 11 countries met inclusion criteria, many of them unpublished. It explains the role of FIND in conducting or sponsoring most studies and gives participant numbers and study periods. Tables summarize study characteristics such as setting, HIV prevalence and reference standards.

blocks.title: Assessment of methodological quality
blocks.content:
The quality of the included studies was appraised with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic 
Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2) tool.10 QUADAS-2 consists of four domains: patient selection, index 
test, reference standard, and flow and timing. All domains were assessed for the potential for risk 
of bias, and the first three domains for concerns regarding applicability. Signalling questions in 
each domain were used to form judgements about the risk of bias. Overall, the risk of bias was 
considered to be high because of problems with the culture-based reference standard (all studies), 
unclear patie

summary.text: Reports the QUADAS-2 appraisal of the included TB-LAMP studies, judging overall risk of bias as high mainly because of the culture reference standard, unclear patient selection and flow and timing problems. A table gives each study's risk-of-bias and applicability ratings, and notes explain the judgements.

blocks.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis
blocks.content:
6. Cost-effectiveness analysis
This analysis provides evidence for the cost–effectiveness of TB-LAMP as a replacement test for 
sputum-smear microscopy or as an add-on test to sputum-smear microscopy in the further testing 
of smear-negative patients compared with the standard of care in settings where coverage of the 
Xpert MTB/RIF assay is limited (H. Sohn, Cost, affordability, and cost-effectiveness of TB-LAMP 
assay: report to WHO Guideline Development Group meeting on the TB-LAMP assay, unpublished 
report, January 2016).
For the cost analysis, a bottom-up micro-costing analysis was condu

summary.text: Summarizes a costing study of TB-LAMP and Xpert MTB/RIF in peripheral laboratories in Malawi and Viet Nam, comparing TB-LAMP strategies with microscopy-based care. It gives per-test costs and affordability and cost-effectiveness findings, and cautions policy-makers to weigh feasibility and costs before adoption.

blocks.title: Summary: from evidence to recommendations
blocks.content:
The accuracy of TB-LAMP performed directly on sputum samples for diagnosing pulmonary TB 
among adults who have not received TB treatment within 60 days of enrolment was determined 
from 13 studies performed in countries with intermediate and high burdens of TB.

summary.text: Introduces the evidence-to-recommendation summary, noting that TB-LAMP accuracy on sputum was determined from 13 studies in intermediate- and high-burden countries.

blocks.title: TB-LAMP for the detection of pulmonary TB in all adults
blocks.content:
Using data from the 1 810 persons with signs and symptoms consistent with TB for whom the most 
stringent reference standard could be used (Standard 1), TB-LAMP had a pooled sensitivity that 
was 15% higher than smear microscopy (78% compared with 63%). Although pooled specificity 
estimates for TB-LAMP were 2% lower (98% compared with 100%), this may be partly explained 
by the identification of TB cases who were misclassified as TB-negative by the use of culture as a 
reference standard, which varied across studies. All included studies were considered to have a high 
risk of bias in the use

summary.text: Explains the Guideline Development Group's reasoning on TB-LAMP for all adults: higher sensitivity than microscopy with slightly lower specificity, partly attributed to culture misclassification. It weighs the extra cases detected per 1 000 tested against false positives and concludes the trade-off is acceptable.

blocks.title: TB-LAMP for the detection of pulmonary TB in adults living with HIV
blocks.content:
Data from 4 studies (271 participants) that included HIV-positive adults with signs and symptoms 
consistent with pulmonary TB and that evaluated the accuracy of TB-LAMP demonstrated 
sensitivity and specificity similar to sputum-smear microscopy (sensitivity: 64% for TB-LAMP and 
62% for smear microscopy; specificity: 99% for TB-LAMP and 99% for smear microscopy)(Annex 
2, Table 11). Based on this limited dataset, similar numbers of true-positive, false-negative, false-
positive and true-negative results would be obtained using either TB-LAMP or sputum-smear 
microscopy. Although it would be

summary.text: Reports that in a small HIV-positive group TB-LAMP performed about the same as smear microscopy, and explains why the group made no specific recommendation for people living with HIV, citing limited evidence.

blocks.title: TB-LAMP as a replacement test for the Xpert MTB/RIF assay for detecting pulmonary TB in adults
blocks.content:
TB in adults
Although better than microscopy, the pooled sensitivity of TB-LAMP is lower than what has been 
reported for the Xpert MTB/RIF assay (89%; 95% credible interval: 85–92).11 The specificity of all 
three tests is similar. In head-to-head comparisons, TB-LAMP appeared to be less sensitive than 
the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, but the difference in sensitivity was not statistically significant except 
when using the least stringent reference standard. More data are needed to confirm that TB-LAMP 
sensitivity is lower than that of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay. It is also important to consider that

summary.text: Compares TB-LAMP with Xpert MTB/RIF, noting lower sensitivity and no rifampicin resistance detection, and explains why Xpert remains preferred where resources allow while TB-LAMP may suit peripheral sites.

blocks.title: WHO policy recommendations
blocks.content:
8. WHO policy recommendations
Given the GRADE evidence assessment and considering the relative benefits and harms associated 
with the use of the TB-LAMP, WHO recommends the following.
1.  TB-LAMP may be used as a replacement test for sputum-smear microscopy to diagnose 
pulmonary TB in adults with signs and symptoms consistent with TB (conditional 
recommendation, very low-quality evidence).
2.  TB-LAMP may be used as a follow-on test to smear microscopy in adults with signs and 
symptoms consistent with pulmonary TB, especially when further testing of sputum smear-
negative specimens is ne

summary.text: States WHO's two conditional recommendations, based on very low-quality evidence, for TB-LAMP as a replacement for or follow-on to smear microscopy in symptomatic adults. Remarks restrict their use to sputum, caution against replacing rapid rifampicin-resistance tests and note uncertainty for people with HIV and extrapolation to children.

blocks.title: Implementation considerations
blocks.content:
9. Implementation considerations
The systematic review supports the use of TB-LAMP as a replacement test for smear microscopy 
for diagnosing pulmonary TB in countries with an intermediate or high burden of TB. However, the 
Xpert MTB/RIF assay should remain the preferred diagnostic for all persons suspected of having 
TB, providing there are sufficient resources and infrastructure to support its use, given the evidence, 
its ability to simultaneously identify rifampicin resistance and because it is automated.
•  Several operational issues accompany the implementation of TB-LAMP: the needs fo

summary.text: Lists implementation considerations for TB-LAMP, including electricity, storage temperature, waste disposal and stock needs. It also notes that smear microscopy is still needed for treatment monitoring and that Xpert MTB/RIF should not be replaced.

blocks.title: Plans for disseminating WHO’s guidance on TB-LAMP
blocks.content:
10. Plans for disseminating WHO’s guidance on TB-LAMP 
This WHO guidance will be published online (http://www.who.int/tb/publications/lamp-diagnosis-
molecular/en/) and disseminated through WHO’s Global TB Department listserv to all WHO Regional 
and Country Offices and Member States, the Global Laboratory Initiative, the New Diagnostics 
Working Group of the Stop TB Partnership, and donors, technical agencies and other stakeholders.

summary.text: Describes how the TB-LAMP guidance will be published online and distributed to WHO offices, Member States and partner networks.

blocks.title: Research needs
blocks.content:
11. Research needs 
The current recommendations for the commercial TB-LAMP manual assay should not prevent or 
restrict further research on new TB diagnostics, especially point-of-care assays that can be used 
as close as possible to where patients access TB treatment. Additional studies using standardized 
protocols that include a high-quality culture reference standard (liquid culture results on at least 
two samples) are needed to better inform national TB programmes of the relative performance of 
TB-LAMP compared with the the Xpert MTB/RIF assay. Further operational research on TB-LAMP 
s

summary.text: Lists research needs for TB-LAMP, such as studies with stronger culture reference standards, evaluation of diagnostic algorithms, training needs, patient impact and country-specific cost analyses.
